newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. envoy threatens to leave Israel-PLO talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy threatens to leave Israel-PLO talks.

text.p: A U.S. envoy threatened to leave the Middle East on Monday unless Israel and the PLO made dramatic progress on a Hebron peace deal, PLO and diplomatic sources said.

Dennis Ross, dispatched by U.S. President Bill Clinton 15 days ago after an eruption of violence, told Palestinian President Yasser Arafat he planned to leave on Monday, PLO negotiator Hassan Asfour said.
"Ross informed Arafat and the Palestinians on Saturday night that if there was no progress on Sunday night he planned to leave for Washington. He had other things to work on," Asfour told Reuters.

"It's a good possibility," said a diplomatic source when asked about Asfour's comment. Ross scheduled a news conference for 1400 GMT on Monday just after he was due to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The diplomatic source said that meeting, attended also by Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, would be crucial to Ross's decision whether to return to the United States, where Clinton is seeking re-election on November 5.

Israel and the PLO are trying to clinch a deal to implement a long-promised Israeli troop pullback from Hebron, the last and most sensitive of seven West Bank cities due to be handed over to Palestinian rule in a 1995 peace accord.

An outbreak of West Bank and Gaza violence that claimed the lives of 60 Arabs and 15 Israelis prompted Clinton to call a White House summit attended by Netanyahu and Arafat and send Ross to the region.
The PLO official said Washington would continue to be represented in the talks by U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk and U.S. Consul General in East Jerusalem Edward Abington.
The diplomatic source, who declined to be identified, said Ross might want to leave early to avoid devaluing his influence by continuing to participate in slow-moving negotiations.

"If things cannot be done immediately he (Ross) would come back when the parties get closer...There aren't that many things left which have to be resolved. It's a matter of hammering the language out on paper," the source said.

Clinton despatched Ross, a veteran Middle East peace broker, to ensure implementation of the Hebron accord held up since March by Islamic suicide bombings and Netanyahu's concern for the security of 400 Jews living in enclaves in the heart of the West Bank city among 100,000 Arabs.

Netanyahu, who turned 47 on Monday, ousted Nobel peace laureate Shimon Peres, 73, in an election in May. He opposes the foundation of five years of peace talks -- Israel swapping occupied Arab land for peace.
French President Jacques Chirac, on a seven-day tour of the region aimed at increasing a European role in Arab-Israeli peace moves, arrived on Monday in Jerusalem where he met President Ezer Weizman.
